li.a: The Texas Tribune: Horror in El Paso: 20 dead, 26 wounded in mass shooting at Walmart

content.p: El Paso is a border city, and NPR reported that about 80 percent of its residents are of Mexican descent. On the morning of Saturday 3 August 2019 a Walmart on the city's east side was busy with back-to-school shoppers. Police said the first emergency calls came in at about 10 a.m. A man had opened fire at the store, and by Monday the death toll stood at 22. Later reporting, including NPR's in 2025, counts 23 dead. NPR calls it one of the deadliest mass shootings in US history.

The suspect, 21-year-old Patrick Crusius of Allen, a suburb of Dallas, was arrested shortly after the shooting began. An anti-immigrant, anti-Hispanic online post was linked to him by authorities and the press. He was charged with capital murder by the state and, years later, pleaded guilty to federal hate crime charges; NPR reported that he had already been sentenced to 90 consecutive life sentences by March 2025. In March 2025 the El Paso County district attorney announced an offer under which he would avoid a state death sentence.

The Walmart stands beside Interstate 10, and NPR described it as a popular destination among Mexican tourists who cross from Juárez. CBS News reported that the shopping area is about five miles from the main border checkpoint. Among the customers were Andre and Jordan Anchondo and their 2-month-old son, Paul. NPR reported that they had dropped by for school supplies and food for a family barbecue marking their first wedding anniversary and their daughter's sixth birthday.

Survivors' accounts in the Texas Tribune describe the chaos inside the store. One shopper, Victoria Hankins, said she heard seven or eight shots in quick succession, that everyone dropped to the floor and crawled, and that people crowded into a metal shipping container at the back of the store in the heat. In a 2022 Tribune profile, a bank employee who asked to be identified only as Jamie, then 23 and nearly nine months pregnant, described crawling into the bank's vault room with colleagues as the firing went on. The Tribune noted that several news reports said the store manager and other employees had ushered people toward the back so they could leave by the rear doors.

The Tribune's 2022 retelling reported that emergency dispatchers logged the first report of an active shooter at 10:39 a.m., while Sgt. Gomez had put the first calls at about 10 a.m. The sources do not reconcile the two times.

Not everyone ran. Glendon Oakley, a US soldier from Fort Bliss who was at the nearby mall, told a CBS affiliate that he saw many children without their parents and grabbed as many as he could. Andre Anchondo, 23, was killed, and NPR reported that his wife Jordan, 24, died shielding their baby, Paul, who was grazed by a bullet and survived with broken fingers.

Gomez said police arrested the man without incident near the Walmart, and that officers did not believe there were other shooters. According to the arrest warrant affidavit, quoted by NPR, he surrendered as he was driving away, saying "I'm the shooter", and later told investigators that he had planned the attack and made the drive from his home with the intention of targeting Mexicans. NPR described the drive as lasting more than 11 hours, while CBS put it at about ten hours.

Police Chief Greg Allen said on Sunday that the suspect was "forthcoming" and "didn't hold anything back". Allen said the weapon had been purchased legally. Crusius was booked on capital murder charges and held without bond. District Attorney Jaime Esparza said on the Sunday, "We will seek the death penalty," adding that the community had "never seen anything like this".

The first count was uncertain. Reports on Saturday said 20 were dead and 26 wounded. On Monday El Paso police announced that one victim had died early that morning and, per CBS, another a little after 10 a.m., bringing the figure to 22. Authorities had said over the weekend that the number could keep climbing. At least seven of the dead were Mexican citizens. Mexico's foreign secretary, Marcelo Ebrard, called the attack "an act of terrorism against the Mexican-American community and Mexican nationals in the United States".
content.h2: The manifesto and the federal response
content.p: NPR wrote that the post, on a website popular in white supremacist circles, is believed to have gone up under 20 minutes before the attack began, and NBC cited a law enforcement official saying it was posted just before the shooting. Police had mentioned a manifesto within hours, saying investigators would study whether the suspect wrote it. The official said the post attacked immigrants in Texas, and CBS reported that its author expressed support for the gunman in the Christchurch, New Zealand attack. CBS on 5 August still described its authorship as "allegedly" Crusius's.

US Attorney John Bash said on 4 August that his office was investigating with a view towards federal hate crime charges and federal firearms charges carrying the death penalty, and that it was treating the shooting as domestic terrorism, a case "designed to intimidate a civilian population". The FBI said the attack "underscores the continued threat posed by domestic violent extremists" and warned that such extremists could be inspired to commit similar acts.

The Tribune placed the shooting after the November 2017 church shooting at Sutherland Springs and the May 2018 attack at Santa Fe High School, calling it the third mass shooting in Texas in under two years. In the hours after the attack another gunman killed nine people in Dayton, Ohio, according to NBC and CBS.

Officials differed on how to describe the El Paso attack. Gov. Greg Abbott initially emphasised mental health, while Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick cited violent video games but also called the shooting "obviously a hate crime". Land Commissioner George P. Bush spoke of "white terrorism", and Sen. Ted Cruz called it a "heinous act of terrorism and white supremacy". Beto O'Rourke, the presidential candidate and former El Paso congressman, said President Trump's rhetoric contributed to racism in the country. President Trump, in remarks reported by NBC, said hate had "no place" in the country but also called it a "mental illness problem". Trump visited El Paso on the Wednesday after the attack, and Tito Anchondo, Andre's brother, told NPR that he believed people were misconstruing Trump's ideas, while saying he would like to talk with him in person.

On 10 October 2019 Crusius pleaded not guilty to capital murder at a three-minute hearing, speaking only twice. NPR noted that the plea contradicted the confession described in police documents. A grand jury had indicted him the month before.

The state case took years. By 2022 the Texas Tribune could still describe him as charged with more than 90 federal crimes alongside state capital murder. NPR reported that he pleaded guilty to hate crime charges in federal court in 2023 and was sentenced to 90 consecutive life sentences. In 2023 he also agreed to pay more than $5 million to the victims, an amount approved by a federal judge. Court records gave no sign that he had significant assets. The Justice Department under the Biden administration took the death penalty off the table in the federal case, without formally explaining why, though prosecutors acknowledged he suffered from schizoaffective disorder.

On 25 March 2025 El Paso County District Attorney James Montoya, who took office in January and was the fourth district attorney to handle the case, announced that Crusius would be offered a plea to capital murder and a sentence of life in prison without parole. Montoya said a majority of victims' relatives wanted the case closed, and that "he will die in prison." A hearing was set for 21 April, with relatives able to give impact statements.

Montoya, a Democrat, said he supported the death penalty and believed Crusius deserved it, while Gov. Abbott said "any shooting like that is what capital punishment is for". His predecessor Bill Hicks said it was not the reasoning he would have followed, but that he could not fault it. Survivor Adria Gonzalez called the decision "a slap in the face for all the victims", while Elise Hoffmann-Taus, whose father Alexander Hoffmann was killed, said, "This is the outcome I wanted." Dean Reckard, whose mother Margie Reckard died, said Crusius deserved death but that "it's time to put the matter to rest."
content.h2: The people who died, and those who lived on
content.p: NPR described the dead as ranging from a 15-year-old high school athlete to several grandparents, and as including immigrants, a retired city bus driver, teachers and tradesmen. Several were Mexican nationals who had crossed the border on routine shopping trips. The youngest, Javier Amir Rodriguez, was 15 and about to begin his sophomore year at Horizon High School; he had gone to the store with his uncle, who was cashing a paycheck to buy him school clothes.

The aftermath weighed on the living. In October 2019 NPR reported that survivors were facing financial strain and unfamiliar benefit systems, according to Patsy Gomez of the volunteer group Operation H.O.P.E, and that residents were still asking why. Antonio Basco, whose wife of 22 years was killed, drew thousands of strangers to her funeral after a funeral home's online invitation spread, and more than 500 floral arrangements arrived. He was arrested on 30 September 2019 on a driving-while-intoxicated charge while sleeping in a car, NPR reported.

In the weeks before the third anniversary, Jamie visited the El Paso County Healing Garden memorial at Ascarate Park for the first time and told the Tribune she felt at peace. A memorial to the victims stood in the city in March 2025 when the plea offer was announced.
